About The Project
=======================================================================

Column {data-width = 300}
-------------------------
<br> 

#### What Are We Investigating?

The Bureau of Land Management manages 245 million acres of land across the US, measuring a tenth of America's land. While BLM public lands are less visited than national parks, they are known for offering more activities with less restrictions. In 2024, BLM public lands hosted 80 million visitors. Colorado has over 150 BLM public lands sites varying from museums to open wilderness, to trail systems and boat access points. Some dashboards exist for finding public lands based on activities, but they have limited info on filtering sites and measuring characteristics, like the number of activities and description length. 

#### Why Is This Important?

A better dashboard would allow potential visitors to plan trips better-- understanding what different sites have to offer. This dashboard can help data scientists too, by mapping  sites and analyzing whether there are meta-relationships between description length and activity count, among other analysis

+ [BLM Visitor Info](https://www.blm.gov/blog/2025-06-26/blm-public-lands-know-you-go)
+ [BLM Overview](https://www.blm.gov/about/what-we-manage/national)

#### Our Key Questions

What is the primary attraction type of each site and what is the distribution?

What sites have the longest descriptions? Does this correlate to activities offered?

What sites have certain activities?

#### Data Attribution

+ Data from scraped from [BLM Programs](https://www.blm.gov/visit/search?field_location=100035&field_activities=All&search_api_fulltext=&page=) 
+ Visit our [GitHub!](https://github.com/lgnsamuels-26/samuelson-hickman_final_project_SDS264)

### Total Presence of activity

```{r}
ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("Pie Chart of Existence of Activity"),
  
sidebarLayout(
  sidebarPanel(
    selectInput(
      inputId = "xvar",
      label = "Choose a variable:",
      choices = c("CAMPING","WATER SPORTS","ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION","NON-MOTORIZED BOATING","DAY USE AREA","PADDLE BOATING","WATER ACCESS","RAFTING","WHITEWATER RAFTING","BIRDING","BACKPACKING","INTERPRETIVE PROGRAMS","WILDLIFE VIEWING","FISHING","BOATING","HORSEBACK RIDING","HIKING","OFF HIGHWAY VEHICLE","RECREATIONAL VEHICLES","SCENIC DRIVE","PHOTOGRAPHY","CLIMBING","HUNTING","WILDERNESS","INFORMATION SITE","PICNICKING"),
      selected = "camping")),
mainPanel(
    plotOutput("piePlot"))))

server <- function(input, output) {
output$piePlot <- renderPlot({
pie_data <- BLM %>%
  count(value = .data[[input$xvar]]) %>%
  filter(!is.na(value)) %>%
  mutate(
    value = factor(
      value,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c(paste("Proportion Without", input$xvar), paste("Proportion With", input$xvar))))
    
ggplot(pie_data, aes(x = "", y = n, fill = value)) +
  geom_col(color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey", "darkgreen")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Pie Chart of", input$xvar),
    fill = "Status") +
  theme_void()})}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)





```


### Total Presence of Each Activity
```{r}

ui <- fluidPage(
titlePanel("BLM Recreation Activity Counts"),
mainPanel(
  plotOutput("barPlot", height = "700px")))

server <- function(input, output) {
output$barPlot <- renderPlot({
    
activities <- c("CAMPING","WATER SPORTS","ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION",
             "NON-MOTORIZED BOATING","DAY USE AREA","PADDLE BOATING",
           "WATER ACCESS","RAFTING","WHITEWATER RAFTING","BIRDING",
            "BACKPACKING","INTERPRETIVE PROGRAMS","WILDLIFE VIEWING",
            "FISHING","BOATING","HORSEBACK RIDING","HIKING",
            "OFF HIGHWAY VEHICLE","RECREATIONAL VEHICLES","SCENIC DRIVE",
              "PHOTOGRAPHY","CLIMBING","HUNTING","WILDERNESS",
             "INFORMATION SITE","PICNICKING")
    
activity_counts <- data.frame(
  Activity = activities,
  Count = sapply(activities, function(x) {
    sum(BLM[[x]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
      }))

activity_counts <- activity_counts %>%
  arrange(desc(Count))
    
ggplot(activity_counts,
  aes(x = reorder(Activity, Count), y = Count)) +
  geom_col(fill = "darkgreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Total Number of Recreation Sites by Activity",
    x = "Activity",
    y = "Total Instances of Activity") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)})}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
```

### Activity Density Per Location

```{r}
library(sf)
library(mapview)
library(dplyr)

activity_cols <- c("CAMPING","WATER SPORTS","ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION",
             "NON-MOTORIZED BOATING","DAY USE AREA","PADDLE BOATING",
           "WATER ACCESS","RAFTING","WHITEWATER RAFTING","BIRDING",
            "BACKPACKING","INTERPRETIVE PROGRAMS","WILDLIFE VIEWING",
            "FISHING","BOATING","HORSEBACK RIDING","HIKING",
            "OFF HIGHWAY VEHICLE","RECREATIONAL VEHICLES",
              "PHOTOGRAPHY","CLIMBING","HUNTING","WILDERNESS",
             "INFORMATION SITE","PICNICKING")

df <- BLM |>
  filter(Latitude != 0) |>
  mutate(
    activity_count = rowSums(
      across(all_of(activity_cols)) == 1,
      na.rm = TRUE))

points_sdf <- st_as_sf(
  df,
  coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"),
  crs = 4326)

mapview(
  points_sdf,
  zcol = "activity_count",
  cex = "activity_count",
  col.regions = colorRampPalette(c("green", "darkgreen")),
  legend = TRUE,
  label = points_sdf$Name,
  layer.name = "Total Activity Count")
```

Query Colorado Public Land
==========================

Inputs {.sidebar}
-------------------------
```{r, echo=FALSE}

## Sets the activity id used in later calls, the label, which is seen by the viewer, and the choices. Here, we allow for multiple choices, allowing for a multiple filter options.
selectInput(
  inputId = "Activity",
  label = "Select Activities",
  choices = c("CAMPING","WATER SPORTS","ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION",
             "NON-MOTORIZED BOATING","DAY USE AREA","PADDLE BOATING",
           "WATER ACCESS","RAFTING","WHITEWATER RAFTING","BIRDING",
            "BACKPACKING","INTERPRETIVE PROGRAMS","WILDLIFE VIEWING",
            "FISHING","BOATING","HORSEBACK RIDING","HIKING",
            "OFF HIGHWAY VEHICLE","RECREATIONAL VEHICLES","SCENIC DRIVE",
              "PHOTOGRAPHY","CLIMBING","HUNTING","WILDERNESS",
             "INFORMATION SITE","PICNICKING"),
  selected= "DAY USE AREA",
  multiple=TRUE
)
## Sets the attraction type and sorts the choices such that there is an option for each type, plus the ability to select them all. 
selectInput(
  inputId  ="Attraction Type",
  label   = "Attraction Type",
  choices= c("All", sort(unique(BLM$`Attraction Type`))),
  selected= "All"
) 
## Sets the zip code so that users can filter by location. Same logic as above.
selectInput(
  inputId  ="Zip Code",
  label   = "Zip Code",
  choices= c("All", sort(unique(BLM$`Zip Code`))),
  selected= "All"
)
```

Column {.tabset .tabset-fade}
-------------------------

#### Filtered by Activity, Attraction Type, and Zip Code

The following dashboard allows you to search by activity and attraction type. This offers an intuitive way for potential travelers to pinpoint the public land in Colorado best suited for them. Importantly, if shows us that the attraction types, like Campground, do not always contain all lands where camping or an attraction related activity is allowed!
<br>
<br>

```{r}
## The name of this visual is filtered activity
filtered_activity <- reactive({
  BLM_df <- BLM
## If the input is not "All," the input is filtered to the user selection.  
    if (input$`Attraction Type` != "All") {
    BLM_df <- BLM_df |> filter(`Attraction Type` == input$`Attraction Type`)
  }
## If the Activity is not zero, for every column indicated in the query as 1 is added to the data set with a for loop.
if(length(input$Activity) > 0) {
for(col in input$Activity) {
     BLM_df <- BLM_df[BLM_df[[col]] == 1, ]
}
  ## If the Zip Code is specified, the dataset is filtered by the choice.
     if (input$`Zip Code` != "All") {
    BLM_df <- BLM_df |> filter(`Zip Code` == input$`Zip Code`)
  }

  BLM_df
}})

## Rendering the datatable with the DT package. The preset columns are the site name, address, city, zip code, attraction type, total activities, and activities list.
renderDT({
  datatable(
  filtered_activity() |> select(`Name`, Address, City,`Zip Code`, `Attraction Type`, `Total Activities`, Activities),
    options = list(pageLength = 30,
                   scrollY = "600px"),
    rownames = FALSE
  )
})
```


Text Analysis
==========================

Inputs {.sidebar}
-------------------------

```{r}
## This makes at id called "text", where users see "Text Counts." Choices, which are numeric are available.
inputPanel(
      selectInput(inputId = "text",
                  label = h3("Text Counts"),
                  choices = c("Description Character Length",
                              "Description Word Count",
                              "Direction Character Length",
                              "Direction Word Count"),
                  selected = "Description Word Count"))
## This allows the user to select the categorical variables that we want to find distributions for. 
selectInput(
  inputId  ="categ",
  label   = "Filter Sites",
  choices= c("Attraction Type",
             "Zip Code",
             "Contact Region",
             "Total Activities"),
  selected = "Total Activities"
)

```

Column {.tabset .tabset-fade}
-------------------------
There are many activities offered in Colorado public lands, but we ask, is it possible to predict the length of the site description or directions? This leads us to evaluate the distributions by the activity counts per site, the zip code, or the contact region. Contact Region denotes sites that share the same phone number, indicating the same field office. If field offices author these descriptions, there may be patterns of length.
<br>
<br>
```{r, fig.height=8}
renderPlot(
  height = 450,
  {
    BLM |>
    mutate(`Total Activities` = as.factor(`Total Activities`),
           `Zip Code` = as.factor(`Zip Code`),
           `Contact Region` = as.factor(`Contact Region`))|>
    ggplot(aes(y = .data[[input$text]], x = fct_reorder(.data[[input$categ]],.data[[input$text]]), fill = .data[[input$categ]])) +
      geom_boxplot()+
    labs(title = paste(input$text, "vs", input$categ),
           x     = input$categ,
           y     = input$text)+
   theme_minimal()
  
})
```

<br>
<br>
<br>
Results show that there are not strong relationships between the amount of activities offered and description word count. This makes sense considering that sites with few activities, which represent most sites, have a lower and tighter distribution of description word count.

For Contact Regions, which represent sites with the same phone number, there is variation between sites' median description word counts and their spread. This suggests that certain regions, like Region 15, likely have field offices that tend to write more on their sites' webpages.

Zip Codes show some variation, but are less interesting for analysis. Some Zip Codes have more sites than another, similar to Contact Regions, but a field office is a better explanation of this trend than an unrelated geographic boundary.

Filtering by attraction type shows that the campground subtype has a wide spread of word counts across its site descriptions. This may show that there is more variation in the types of descriptions a campground receives. More research could explain if there are campgrounds with more or less amenities or pertinent details to discuss. Or, perhaps campgrounds are spread across contact regions and this explains the variation. 

Direction length, we conclude is very standard across different filters. It seems that this element of the website requires roughly the same amount of information per site.
